_comment: Single source of truth. index.html renders from this file.
_writing: Every description must work for a reader who will NEVER open the product. State the problem, who has it, what the thing actually does, what was hard, and the numbers. No insider shorthand.
_verified: 2026-08-04 — every status checked against a live endpoint or the iTunes Lookup API, not from memory

owner.name: QQ Chen
owner.headline: I deliver enterprise projects by day. At night I ship AI products — eleven this year, three through App Store review.
owner.blurb: Most people who can run a complex delivery programme have never shipped a product themselves. Most people who ship products have never carried enterprise delivery risk. I do both, and the second one is unpaid — I build these on evenings and weekends because this is the work I want to be doing full time.
owner.why: Everything below was built outside working hours. That constraint is the point: with a few hours a night you cannot afford to guess, so every decision here had to be measured, cut, or justified. The habits that produced it are the ones I would bring to leading AI projects.

products.name: TingZhai
products.subtitle: AI notes for podcast listeners
products.tagline: Hands busy? Say "note" out loud and the last 60 seconds is captured, transcribed and filed.
products.role: Solo — product, backend, iOS, App Store submission
products.problem: People listen to podcasts while cooking, driving or running — exactly when reaching for the phone is impossible. So the one good idea per episode is lost. Existing apps require a tap, which means they only work when you weren't really busy.
products.what: An iOS app and web app that plays podcasts and lets you capture a moment by speaking a single word. It rewinds 60 seconds, transcribes that span, has an LLM title and summarise it, then schedules it for spaced review at 1, 3, 7 and 14 days.
products.hard: Two things. First, wake-word detection that runs on-device, works while audio is playing through the same speaker, and does not fire during normal conversation. Second, keeping AI cost viable when every listener processes the same episodes.
highlights: Custom on-device wake word instead of Siri, so playback is never interrupted. Validated against 127,000 characters of real Chinese podcast transcripts: false triggers went from 38 to 0 after switching from single-character matching to a debounced multi-word matcher.
Cross-tenant transcript cache keyed on feed URL plus episode ID: one episode costs AI money once, no matter how many users process it. 86% cache hit rate, 7.07× reuse, US$0.82 per episode all-in.
Spaced repetition (SM-2) on captured highlights — no competing podcast app ships this.

Ran an adversarial pre-submission review with a second AI agent. It caught two real App Store rejection risks I had written myself: a described feature the iOS build did not have, and a privacy label that under-declared audio collection.
products.business: Free tier: 3 hours of AI processing per month. Pro: NT$399/month for 30 hours. Unit economics verified — worst-case cost per Pro user stays under revenue.

products.name: Woordjes
products.subtitle: Dutch vocabulary for exam candidates
products.tagline: 2,000 high-frequency Dutch words, levelled A1/A2/B1, with spaced repetition.
products.role: Solo — product, backend, iOS, App Store submission
products.problem: Dutch integration-exam candidates are mostly adults studying around a job. Generic vocabulary apps teach words they will never be tested on, and Dutch-specific material for Chinese speakers barely exists.
products.what: An iOS and web app with an original 2,000-word deck built from frequency data and the official exam syllabus, illustrated where illustration helps, scheduled by spaced repetition.
products.hard: Deciding what to teach. Frequency lists alone give you function words; syllabus lists alone give you words nobody says. The deck is the intersection, levelled so a beginner never meets a rare word early.
highlights: Concrete nouns are auto-illustrated with generated images — roughly 300 images for about US$2, because abstract words are the ones illustration cannot help.
Frequency-based levelling so the first 200 words carry the most conversational weight.
The engine was later reused for a Japanese app with 95% code shared — only the content layer differs. Proving that took shipping the second app, not arguing about it.
products.business: Free, no ads, no tracking. Built as a tool for my own exam; the App Store listing exists so other candidates can find it.

products.name: Tango
products.subtitle: Japanese vocabulary, JLPT N5–N1
products.tagline: 10,000 words levelled by corpus frequency instead of by intuition.
products.role: Solo — product, backend, iOS, App Store submission
products.problem: JLPT decks are usually levelled by hand or inherited from old lists. The failure mode is invisible: advanced compounds get filed as intermediate, so learners hit words they cannot possibly know and conclude they are bad at Japanese.
products.what: An iOS and web app covering N5 through N1 vocabulary plus grammar cards, on one spaced-repetition scheduler.
products.hard: This was a data problem, not an app problem. An earlier heuristic had quietly pushed advanced kanji compounds down into N3. I rebuilt levelling against a 44,000-word frequency corpus so that how common a word is decides its level.
highlights: Full deck re-levelled against corpus frequency; leakage of N1 vocabulary into lower levels dropped to zero, and the N3 bucket shrank from 39% to 21% of the deck.
Grammar and vocabulary share one scheduler, so a review session mixes both the way a real exam does.
Second product off the same engine as Woordjes — shipping it was content work, not a rewrite.
products.business: Free. Serves as the proof that the vocabulary engine generalises across languages.

products.name: Dutch PlayPhrase
products.subtitle: Learn Dutch from real video, not textbooks
products.tagline: Search 700,000 real Dutch subtitle lines and hear each one spoken in context.
products.problem: Textbook Dutch is not the Dutch anyone speaks. Learners can recite a phrase and still not recognise it at native speed, because they have only ever heard it read aloud slowly by one voice.
products.what: A searchable index of 700,000 subtitle lines from Dutch video. Type a word or phrase and you get every clip where a real person says it, played back at native speed with the transcript aligned. Adds a vocabulary notebook with spaced review and A2/KNM mock exams on top.
products.hard: Search relevance across a corpus this size where the useful result is not the best keyword match but the clearest, most natural-sounding utterance. Plus keeping playback instant when clips live on someone else's infrastructure.
highlights: Full learning loop rather than a lookup toy: search → listen → save to notebook → spaced review → mock exam.
Together with Woordjes and the practice hub, this is the most complete Dutch exam-prep resource available to Chinese-speaking learners — a market no existing product serves.
Deployment lesson learned the hard way: pushing to git does not deploy, and container env changes need an explicit redeploy. Both are now written into the repo's runbook.
products.business: Free while the corpus grows. The exam-prep layer is the natural paid tier.

products.name: MaiLuo
products.subtitle: Turns an article into the argument behind it
products.tagline: Not a summary — a map of how the author actually got from premise to conclusion.
products.problem: Summaries tell you what a piece said. They do not tell you why the author believed it, which is the part you need in order to disagree with it, build on it, or remember it a month later.
products.what: Paste a Markdown document or a YouTube link. It splits the content into claim cards and draws edges between them — but an edge is only drawn when the system can state the reason for it. The output is the reasoning path, plus a short and a long reading track and generated audio.
products.hard: Making the model refuse to connect things. The easy version draws a pretty graph where everything relates to everything, which is worthless. Requiring a stated justification per edge is what makes the output trustworthy.
highlights: Every edge carries its reason. Connections the model cannot justify are not drawn at all.
Two reading depths generated in one pass, plus text-to-speech for commute listening.
Four follow-up actions on any card: enrich it, health-check it, borrow it into another board, or diagram it.
products.business: Invite-only while the edge-justification quality is tuned. Positioned as a paid research tool, not a consumer app.

products.name: Language Practice Hub
products.subtitle: Dutch A2 speaking-exam prep
products.tagline: Seventeen worked past papers for an exam almost nobody publishes material for.
products.problem: The Dutch A2 speaking exam has two very different question types and almost no published practice material in Chinese. Candidates walk in having never rehearsed the actual format.
products.what: Seventeen worked past-paper sets with model answers and response templates, a 14-day sprint plan, and a daily review queue.
products.hard: Structuring the content. Early drafts mixed the two question types together and were unusable — the two demand different preparation, so they had to be kept structurally separate throughout.
highlights: Picture-response questions always ship with the actual image. A written description of a picture is not practice.
Free teaser version is public; the complete set is the paid product, kept out of version control so it cannot leak by accident.
Part of the most complete Dutch exam-prep set available to Chinese-speaking candidates.
products.business: Free preview publicly; the full 17-paper set is sold as a paid resource.

products.name: Yike
products.subtitle: A journal with room for exactly one thing
products.tagline: One entry a day. Each one grows a tree; the forest is the evidence you showed up.
products.problem: To-do apps optimise for volume, so people record everything and review nothing. What actually helps is a record of the one thing that mattered — but no product makes that the constraint.
products.what: A journalling PWA and iOS app with a single slot per day. Each entry grows a tree, and the accumulated forest is a visual record of consistency over months.
products.hard: Resisting gamification. Forest-style apps use the tree as bait to make you stay off your phone. Here the tree has to be evidence rather than a reward, or the whole premise collapses into another streak app.
highlights: The tree is proof of depth, not a reward loop — a deliberate design decision made after studying how Forest uses the same visual.
Gumroad licence keys activate automatically through a Supabase edge function, so purchases need no manual step.
Ships as an installable PWA and a native iOS build from one codebase.
products.business: Free to use; sync across devices is a paid upgrade, delivered via Gumroad licence keys.

products.name: Miraa
products.subtitle: Pronunciation practice by echo drilling
products.tagline: Listen three seconds, say it back, get scored word by word — not sentence by sentence.
products.problem: Speaking apps score a whole sentence and return one number. That tells a learner they were wrong but not which syllable, so they repeat the same mistake with more confidence.
products.what: A drill that plays a three-second span, records the learner repeating it, and scores each word individually against the reference. Adds dictation mode, spaced repetition and Japanese furigana annotation.
products.hard: Mobile web audio. Recording and playback in the same session on iOS fails in ways that look like bugs in your code but are platform behaviour.
highlights: Per-word scoring rather than one number per sentence, so the learner knows exactly what to fix.

Solved two iOS web-audio traps that silently break recording: reusing a gesture-unlocked audio element stops working after the first playback, and MediaRecorder returns empty blobs unless started with a timeslice.
Twenty build iterations before the drill felt right — the interaction, not the model, was the hard part.
products.business: Invite-gated while scoring accuracy is validated with real learners.

products.name: Yicheng
products.subtitle: A work log that records what you learned
products.tagline: Projects, tasks, and the thing the work taught you — the third axis most logs drop.
products.problem: Work logs record output. Six months later that tells you that you were busy, not that you got better. The learning is the part worth keeping and the part every tool omits.
products.what: A three-axis log — project, task, and what it taught you — running entirely in the browser with no account and no server.
products.hard: Nothing technically. The design constraint was the point: zero backend means there is no data to breach and no service to keep running, which is the right trade for a private journal.
highlights: localStorage only — no account, no server, nothing to leak.
Three-axis structure instead of a flat task list, so the record answers 'what did I learn' and not only 'what did I do'.
products.business: Free, private by construction. Companion to Yike rather than a separate product line.

products.name: Gongdu
products.subtitle: Group check-in for an early-rising reading club
products.tagline: You can see whether your group is up yet. That turns out to be the entire mechanism.
products.problem: Solo reading habits collapse in about two weeks. Group accountability fixes it, but group chat is the wrong surface — it is noisy and there is no glanceable state.
products.what: A shared check-in wall that syncs in real time. One tap to check in; the board shows who is already up.
products.hard: Almost nothing, and that is the point — the product is one well-chosen mechanic, shipped in a weekend, which is why the group actually uses it.
highlights: Real-time sync via Supabase so the board updates without a refresh.
Sunrise theme: the earlier you check in, the brighter the board gets — the reward is visual and immediate.
products.business: Free. Built for one real group that still uses it.

products.name: YuQiao
products.subtitle: AI-assisted language exchange
products.tagline: The AI feeds you words until you no longer need it, then gets out of the way.
products.role: Solo — product, backend. Built in one night.
products.problem: The hard part of language exchange is not vocabulary, it is the silence in the first ten minutes. Most people quit before they ever get past it.
products.what: A real-time voice room for two learners with an AI in the middle supplying words, prompts and topics — and stepping back automatically once the humans find their rhythm.
products.hard: Defining success backwards. The AI is working when its own usage declines, which means the product has to measure its own irrelevance.
highlights: Success metric is inverted: fewer AI interventions per session over time means the bridge worked.
Real-time voice rooms with sub-second turn handoff.
Built end to end in a single night as a test of whether the premise held at all.
products.business: Experimental. Kept live because the premise is worth testing with real pairs, not because it is a business yet.

approach.title: I make AI agents review each other, and I verify before I trust them
approach.body: I run Claude and Codex on the same repository under one written protocol: reviewer is never the author, and only the reviewer can close a ticket. Before trusting the second agent I ran a four-stage validation on it — including a deliberate trap asking it to close its own ticket with a plausible excuse.
approach.evidence: It refused, citing the rule by line number. That result told me the document-level constraint was sufficient and saved me from building an enforcement layer I had already scoped.

approach.title: The most valuable review is the one that catches me
approach.body: On the submission before App Store review, the second agent audited work I had written myself.
approach.evidence: It found two real rejection risks: a feature described in the store listing that the iOS build did not actually have, and a privacy label declaring no audio collection while a paid feature uploaded recordings. Both were mine. Both were caught before submission.

approach.title: AI cost is an architecture decision, not a billing surprise
approach.body: Per-user AI processing does not survive contact with growth. I keyed a cross-tenant cache on content identity rather than user identity, so an episode costs money once no matter how many people process it.
approach.evidence: 86% cache hit rate, 7.07× reuse, US$0.82 all-in per hour of audio — measured, not estimated. Unit economics verified against the paid tier before pricing it.

approach.title: I measure the thing I am afraid of, on real data
approach.body: A voice trigger that fires during normal speech is worse than no voice trigger. Rather than tuning by feel, I replayed 127,000 characters of real podcast transcripts through the matcher.
approach.evidence: First run: 38 false triggers. After removing single-character matches and adding a debounce, zero — on the same corpus. The same discipline re-levelled a 10,000-word JLPT deck against a 44,000-word frequency corpus.

approach.title: Deciding not to build is part of the job
approach.body: Keeping a voice mode alive on a locked screen was technically possible and I had the design ready. I worked through who would actually use it and what it cost in battery.
approach.evidence: Two existing paths already covered both real scenarios, so I did not build it and wrote down why. The same call killed an agent-enforcement layer after testing showed it was unnecessary.

approach.title: Claims get verified against reality, including my own
approach.body: Every status on this page was checked against a live endpoint or the App Store API on the day it was published — not written from memory.
approach.evidence: That habit exists because a status board I maintained once said four features were shipped when the branch had never been merged. A board that lies is worse than no board, because you act on it.
